scalar.d: A single ordinary number, as opposed to a vector or a matrix. Multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches it: 2·(3, 1) = (6, 2).

linear combination.d: A sum of scaled vectors, like 2a + 3b. A matrix times a vector is a linear combination of the matrix's columns.

column vector.d: A vector written as a vertical column of numbers. A row vector is the same numbers written across. The transpose turns one into the other, and a row times a column is a dot product.

standard basis.d: The unit arrows along the axes: e₁ = (1, 0) and e₂ = (0, 1) in the plane. A matrix's columns are where it sends them.

orthonormal.d: Perpendicular to each other and each of length 1. In an orthonormal basis, each coordinate of a vector is just a dot product with one basis vector.

singular matrix.d: A square matrix with determinant zero. It squashes space onto a line (or smaller), so several inputs share one output and it has no inverse.

shear.d: A map that slides each layer sideways by an amount proportional to its height, like pushing the top of a deck of cards. It never changes area: determinant 1.

orientation.d: Which way round a shape's corners go: anticlockwise or clockwise. A map with negative determinant flips it, like a mirror.

parallelogram.d: A four-sided shape whose opposite sides are parallel and equal. A linear map turns a square into one.

null space.d: All the inputs a matrix sends to zero: the directions it cannot see. For the outer product a·bᵀ it is every vector perpendicular to b.

law of cosines.d: For a triangle with sides A, B and C, where θ is the angle between A and B: C² = A² + B² − 2AB·cos θ. With θ = 90° it is Pythagoras.

Pythagoras' theorem.d: In a right-angled triangle, the long side squared equals the sum of the other two sides squared: 3² + 4² = 5².

off-diagonal.d: Any entry of a square matrix not on the main diagonal: row number and column number differ. In a Hessian these are the interactions.
